notes.meaning: God gave Ezekiel this message in the twelfth year of King Jehoiachin's captivity, in late winter (around March 585 BC). This was shortly after word had reached the exiles in Babylon that Jerusalem had fallen. God told the prophet to speak against Pharaoh, assuring everyone that Egypt could not escape judgment either.

A lament was a funeral song chanted over the dead, and God directed Ezekiel to sing one for Pharaoh while he was still alive. Pharaoh viewed himself as a fierce lion on land, but God called him a thrashing water monster, like a crocodile in the Nile. His proud actions stirred up trouble and disrupted life for the nations all around him.

The Lord announced that He would catch this sea beast using a large fishing net. The net represented the Babylonian army and the many allied nations fighting under King Nebuchadnezzar. Though Pharaoh thought he was untamable, God was fully in control of his capture.

Just as a water creature dies quickly when hauled out of the river onto dry ground, Pharaoh and his power would be helpless on land. God would leave his fallen soldiers unburied in the open fields. Scavenger birds and wild beasts would feast on the corpses of Egypt's proud army.

God gave a vivid picture of the coming slaughter. So many Egyptian soldiers would fall in battle that their dead bodies would cover hills and valleys alike. The huge army that Pharaoh boasted about would become nothing more than rotting piles across the land.

Egypt was famous for the Nile flooding and making the soil fertile, but God warned that a flood of blood would cover the land instead. This echoes the first plague in Exodus, when Egypt's waters turned to blood. The loss of life would be so great that even the dry ravines would be filled.

God described the fall of Pharaoh as putting out a bright light or torch. Cosmic darkness pictures the collapse of a great empire and recalls the plague of darkness that once fell upon Egypt. When God judged the nation, all its royal glory and worldly splendor would suddenly vanish into gloomy sorrow.

The news of Egypt's sudden collapse would shock and distress nations far away. Nearby kings would tremble in fear, realizing that if a mighty power like Egypt could be crushed, their own kingdoms were in danger too. God brandishing His sword shows that He was the true power behind the invading conqueror.

God identified the actual weapon He would use against Egypt: King Nebuchadnezzar and his Babylonian forces. The Babylonians were known as the most ruthless and fierce soldiers of that era. They would strip Egypt of its wealth, crush its armies, and bring its proud reputation to an end.

Egypt's pastures along the Nile would be cleared of cattle, and the busy trade along the river would stop. With so few people or animals left to churn up the riverbanks, the disturbed waters would settle and flow calmly, smooth as olive oil. Pharaoh's restless troublemaking among the nations would finally come to a quiet halt.

The coming devastation would strip Egypt bare of its food, cattle, and crowds of people. Just like during the Exodus generations earlier, this crushing judgment was meant to reveal God's supreme authority. In their defeat, both the Egyptians and the watching world would recognize that the God of Israel is the true and living Lord.

In the ancient world, women were commonly chosen to sing funeral songs over the dead. Here, the "daughters of the nations" represents mourning women from neighboring peoples who would chant this dirge over Egypt's downfall. The ceremony confirmed that the once-mighty empire was truly gone.

Just two weeks after the previous message, God spoke to Ezekiel again in the twelfth month of the same year. This introduced the final funeral song against Egypt in this section of the book. It provided a vivid look at Egypt joining the other fallen world powers in the realm of the dead.

God told Ezekiel to lead the mourning for Egypt's vast population and to send her prophetically down into the grave. In Scripture, when a prophet was told to cast down a nation, it meant he was to announce God's certain decree that it would happen. Egypt would share the same lowly fate as other ruined empires that had gone down into the pit of death.

Ezekiel asked Egypt whether she thought her splendor made her too special to die like everyone else. Despite her royal pride, she would be laid in the dirt with the "uncircumcised," a term meaning godless foreigners who received no honorable burial. Even the most carefully wrapped mummy becomes just another decaying body in the ground.

Egypt was sentenced by God to fall by the sword of enemy invaders. The conquerors are pictured as dragging her and her armies away into disgrace, like dead bodies hauled out to a common grave. No royal honors could protect her people from this sudden ruin.

Sheol refers to the realm of the dead, or the grave. The poem pictures dead warrior kings from past empires welcoming Pharaoh with taunting words as he arrives among them. Pharaoh and his allies had acted like gods on earth, but in the grave they were just as weak and forgotten as any fallen soldier.

Assyria was once the world's most terrifying empire, but she had already been crushed by Babylon and the Medes. Ezekiel describes the king of Assyria buried in the deepest parts of the pit, surrounded by the graves of all his fallen troops. Those who once caused everyone on earth to shudder with fear were now powerless corpses in the dust.

Elam, an ancient and fierce nation east of Babylon famous for its archers, had also been conquered and wiped out. Her soldiers once terrorized the living world, but now they lay in shame among the dishonored dead. Just like Assyria, all their military might could not shield them from God's righteous judgment.

Meshech and Tubal were warlike peoples from the north, located in the region of Asia Minor. Though they were known for brutal violence and instilled deep fear in others, they too had been cut down in battle. They now occupied nameless graves among the rest of the world's ruined armies.

In ancient times, respected heroes were often buried with high military honors, having their swords placed under their heads as pillows. But these violent rulers received no such dignity; they were dumped into common graves with their sins resting heavily upon them. Their former ability to terrorize the living counted for nothing in death.

The message turned directly back to Pharaoh and Egypt. Just as those northern armies were broken and buried without honor, Egypt would be smashed to pieces by the invaders. Pharaoh would have to take his place among the disgraced dead who fell by the sword.

Edom was a neighboring kingdom descended from Esau that had long mocked and mistreated Israel. Despite having proud kings and famous warriors, Edom was destined to be crushed and buried with the conquered. Even though the Edomites practiced circumcision, their hostility to God left them sharing the pit with the uncircumcised heathen.

The northern rulers and the Phoenician sea merchants of Sidon had also boasted in their power and wealth. Yet when destruction came, their strength could not save them, and they were thrown down to the grave in utter humiliation. They now bore their disgrace side by side with all the other fallen nations.

When Pharaoh arrived in the realm of the dead, he would look around and discover all these other mighty monarchs lying in the same dust. It would give him a grim, sorrowful kind of comfort to know he was not alone in his downfall. Yet sharing the pit with other ruined rulers was a pitiful consolation for losing an empire.

Earthly tyrants had terrorized the living world through cruelty, but God would now display His own sovereign terror through His just judgment. Pharaoh and his vast host would certainly be laid to rest in the shame of an unhonored grave. In the end, worldly power fades away, and God alone rules over both the living and the dead.
